stem: Juvenile and adult seals were measured in winter and summer. Basal metabolic rate (BMR) was measured at rest.

parts.label: a
parts.html: (i) Calculate the seasonal difference in mean blubber thickness for adults.

parts.label: a
parts.html: (ii) Calculate adult winter BMR per kilogram.

parts.label: b
parts.html: Compare juvenile and adult seasonal responses.

parts.label: c
parts.html: Explain the winter changes.

parts.label: d
parts.html: Explain why small mammals generally lose heat faster per unit mass.

parts.label: e
parts.html: Evaluate whether the data support a causal effect of season on BMR.

questions.title: Body size and thermal physiology

solparts.label: a
solparts.html: (ii) [1] 9600 kJ day<sup>-1</sup> / 240 kg = 40.0 kJ kg<sup>-1</sup> day<sup>-1</sup>.

solparts.label: b
solparts.html: Both have thicker blubber in winter; juveniles have higher mass-specific BMR; adult mass changes proportionally less between seasons.

solparts.label: c
solparts.html: Thicker blubber reduces heat loss; increased metabolic rate generates heat; food availability/energy storage can increase mass.

solparts.label: d
solparts.html: They have a larger surface-area-to-volume ratio; more surface is exposed per unit tissue; heat transfer to surroundings is therefore faster relative to metabolic volume.

solparts.label: e
solparts.html: There is an association in both age groups; paired/repeated measurements would strengthen inference; uncontrolled food/activity/hormones may confound; experimental temperature control and larger replicated samples are needed for causation.

questions.title: Amino acids and protein structure

solparts.label: a
solparts.html: Essential amino acids must be obtained from food because humans cannot synthesize enough; non-essential amino acids can be synthesized.

solparts.label: b
solparts.html: A central carbon is bonded to an amino group, carboxyl group, hydrogen and variable R group.

solparts.label: c
solparts.html: Hydrogen bonds form between polar groups/backbone and stabilize secondary/tertiary structure; oppositely charged R groups form ionic attractions; disruption by pH/temperature can denature the protein.

questions.title: Muscle fibres and contraction

solparts.label: a
solparts.html: Aerobic respiration produces ATP; ATP powers cross-bridge cycling, Ca2+ pumping and other active processes.

solparts.label: b
solparts.html: Ca2+ exposes actin binding sites; myosin heads bind and perform power strokes using ATP; actin slides past myosin and sarcomeres shorten without filaments shortening.

solparts.label: c
solparts.html: Keeps thick filaments centred; provides elasticity/restores sarcomere length; prevents overstretching.

questions.title: Sustainable harvest and pollutants

solparts.label: a
solparts.html: Measure population size/recruitment and mortality over time; set harvest below replacement at the point of greatest population growth and monitor/adapt quotas.

solparts.label: b
solparts.html: Persistent pollutant is absorbed by producers; not readily excreted/degraded; consumers eat many contaminated organisms so concentration rises at higher trophic levels.

solparts.label: c
solparts.html: It increases mutation/cancer or damages gametes/embryos; survival or reproductive success falls.

solparts.label: d
solparts.html: Eukarya / Eukaryota.

stem: Desert organisms experience low, unpredictable rainfall and high daytime temperatures.
Answer 2 of the following questions. One additional construction mark is available for each response.

parts.html: Define biome.

parts.label: b
parts.html: Explain three plant adaptations to desert conditions.

parts.label: c
parts.html: State one defence against herbivory.

questions.title: Hot desert biome

solparts.label: a
solparts.html: A group/large region of ecosystems with similar climate and characteristic communities/vegetation.

solparts.label: b
solparts.html: Any three linked adaptations: extensive roots increase water uptake; succulent tissues store water; reduced leaves/thick cuticle/sunken stomata reduce transpiration; CAM separates CO2 uptake to night.

solparts.label: c
solparts.html: Spines/thorns, toxins or stinging hairs.

stem: Biological diversity exists in molecules, cells and whole organisms.

parts.label: a
parts.html: Explain the diversity of possible nucleotide sequences.

parts.label: b
parts.html: Describe diversity of protein form and function.

parts.label: c
parts.html: Explain how chromosome fusion can contribute to reproductive isolation.

questions.title: Diversity at multiple levels

solparts.label: a
solparts.html: Four bases can occur at each position; sequence length varies; the number of possible sequences grows as 4<sup>n</sup>; mutation/recombination create new combinations.

solparts.label: b
solparts.html: Different amino acid sequences; variable chain length; folding into secondary/tertiary/quaternary structures; R-group interactions; post-translational modification; examples of enzymes, receptors, antibodies and structural proteins.

solparts.label: c
solparts.html: Fusion changes chromosome number/arrangement; hybrids may have meiotic pairing problems; unbalanced gametes reduce fertility; gene flow falls; populations diverge to form separate species.

solution: Construction [1] Award for a coherent, logically ordered response using appropriate biological terminology.

questions.title: Interactions with molecules and pathogens

solparts.label: a
solparts.html: Inhibitor resembles substrate and binds the active site; blocks substrate binding; lowers rate at a given substrate concentration; effect can be reduced by increasing substrate concentration.

solparts.label: b
solparts.html: Action potential arrives; Ca2+ channels open; Ca2+ enters; vesicles fuse and release acetylcholine; diffusion and receptor binding open ion channels; acetylcholinesterase ends the signal.

solparts.label: c
solparts.html: HIV infects helper T cells using specific receptors; viral replication destroys/reduces them; B-cell activation and cytotoxic T-cell responses decline; opportunistic infections become more likely.

solution: Construction [1] Award for a coherent, logically ordered response using appropriate biological terminology.

stem: Organisms use molecular proofreading and physiological feedback to limit change.

parts.label: a
parts.html: Explain how DNA replication errors are minimized.

parts.label: b
parts.html: Explain hormonal control of blood glucose.

parts.label: c
parts.html: Explain osmoregulation by ADH.

questions.title: Maintaining biological stability

solparts.label: a
solparts.html: Complementary base pairing guides nucleotide addition; DNA polymerase proofreads; mismatches are removed/replaced; repair enzymes correct damage after replication.

solparts.label: b
solparts.html: High glucose stimulates beta cells/insulin, uptake and glycogenesis; low glucose stimulates alpha cells/glucagon, glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis; antagonistic hormones restore the set range by negative feedback.

solparts.label: c
solparts.html: Osmoreceptors detect low water potential; posterior pituitary releases ADH; collecting ducts gain aquaporins; more water is reabsorbed; concentrated urine forms and ADH falls when water potential recovers.

solution: Construction [1] Award for a coherent, logically ordered response using appropriate biological terminology.
